prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of one DNA base into another without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: After the first round I keep base editing as my preferred single-part prize. The scientific case is unchanged and, I think, sharpened by the discussion. The achievement is a chemical reaction made programmable on a genome: an engineered deaminase is tethered to a nickase-type Cas9, one nucleobase is converted in place, and cellular repair completes the change. The adenine editor is the decisive step for the citation, because no natural enzyme deaminates adenine in DNA and the Liu laboratory had to evolve one. That is a result with a clear principle, quantitative evidence of product purity and indel suppression, and independent reproduction in a very large number of laboratories. It created a capability that did not exist, precise single-base change without a double-strand break, and it is now in first-in-human use. I would keep the citation tied to the 2016-2017 discovery and leave prime editing and later engineering outside it.
statement.case_against: The round-1 exchange did not remove the three costs I named. First, proximity to the 2020 CRISPR-Cas9 prize: Sparr, Aqvist and Somfai each put this as a worry that base editing is an application layer on a recognised tool, and I accept that it is the main reason a member could vote against it. Second, attribution: Target-AID by Nishida and Kondo is a real parallel cytosine-editor result, and Zou is right that a trio from one laboratory is a deliberate narrowing. Third, the clinical record is young and bystander editing and long-term safety are still being measured. Against that, B012 is chemically new but cannot be written as one citation with three names, and B055 is the most mature and cleanly attributed option but carries the 2010 overlap and the unsettled Kosugi history.

responses.point: Zou ranked base editing fourth and objects that a Liu, Komor, Gaudelli trio draws only from one laboratory, ignoring the independent Kondo and Nishida Target-AID work.
responses.response: This is the most serious attribution objection and I have changed how I frame it, though not the names. Target-AID is a genuine parallel discovery of the cytosine editor, and I do not want the citation to deny that. But the prize-defining difference is the adenine editor: it needed an enzyme that does not exist in nature to be evolved to act on DNA, and no parallel work from the Japanese group has an adenine counterpart. A citation about programmable base conversion in general would sit uneasily with leaving out Kondo and Nishida, so I would accept that the committee records Target-AID in the background and that this is the cost of the three-name limit. If Zou or others think a pure cytosine-editor priority claim outweighs the adenine step, I would like to hear the argument, because that is where my preference could weaken toward B012.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks base editing fifth, would credit Liu alone, and in his B012 case insists on Handa rather than Ciulli because cereblon explains why thalidomide-type drugs degrade proteins.
responses.response: On Liu alone, I still prefer the trio. Komor made the first cytosine editors and Gaudelli carried the adenine editor through the evolution campaign, and in this case the experimental steps were the discovery, not routine execution. A committee can legitimately choose Liu alone, but then the citation loses the evolved enzyme, which is the strongest chemistry in the field. On B012 you have changed my mind on one point: the cereblon mechanism is a clear and separate result, and Handa's claim for explaining the thalidomide family is stronger than I treated it in round 1. I still rate Ciulli's ternary-complex and VHL ligand work as what made PROTACs drug-like, so for the third name I would now call the choice between Handa and Ciulli a real toss-up, and that makes B012 harder to state as one achievement.

responses.point: Somfai asks what was new chemically in base editing, since cytidine and adenosine deamination are known enzyme reactions, and he regards the work as high-quality protein engineering close to biology.
responses.response: The deamination reactions are indeed known. What was new is the use of that chemistry as a programmable, site-selective reaction on a defined base in the genome, and, for adenine, an evolved catalyst for a reaction no natural enzyme performs on DNA. I would call that chemistry-by-evolution rather than pure biology, in the same spirit as recognising the directed evolution of enzymes in 2018. I accept that this is closer to chemical biology than to a new bond-forming reaction, which is exactly why B055 remains a legitimate rival, and I take his own B055 case seriously on synthetic merit.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks Buchwald and Hartwig first, argues the clinical record of base editing is early and that the enabling idea of programmable targeting was recognised in 2020.
responses.response: I agree that maturity is the right axis and that B055 wins on it: over twenty-five years of independent confirmation and a clean two-name attribution. I do not agree that the CRISPR overlap is the same kind of problem as the 2010 overlap for C-N coupling, since 2020 recognised programmable cleavage and base editing is the avoidance of cleavage with a different chemical event. Still, your point and Somfai's both turn on how much weight the committee gives to continuation of a recognised idea, and that applies to both B055 and B060. Where I remain unconvinced is that the unsettled Kosugi history has been placed on the record, and I would not want to vote for a B055 citation until it has.

responses.point: Chabes shares my first choice and sharpens Target-AID as a cytidine-deaminase result without an adenine counterpart.
responses.response: I agree with the configuration and with the reason for excluding Target-AID from the names, but we both should be careful not to overstate it as a clean exclusion. Maturity by independent confirmation is satisfied for base editing and, as you argue to Aqvist, is not obviously better for B055 than for B060. The remaining weakness is the CRISPR proximity argument, and I would rather the committee face that directly than hide behind the Target-AID technicality.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts base editing as sufficiently distinct from the 2020 CRISPR-Cas9 prize, or reads it as continuation of the same story.
Whether excluding Nishida and Kondo can be defended on the adenine-editor step alone, or whether a cytosine-editor priority claim requires a different configuration.
Whether Kosugi's tin-amide coupling anticipated the ligand-controlled cycle strongly enough to alter a B055 citation; this is not settled in the files.
Whether the committee will credit Handa or Ciulli as the third B012 name, and whether the resulting citation describes one achievement or two.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on B060, B012 or B055. I am a nanophysicist at Lund with no tie to the Liu, Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo, Nishida, Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli, Handa, Buchwald or Hartwig groups. As chair I disclose that my own preferred configuration is among those summarised, and Somfai and Sparr are Lund colleagues with no tie to these candidates. No change from round 1.
